detail.extracted_title: The Gates of Muscat and the Forgotten Logbook: 1763 Oman Survival (Part III)
detail.excerpt: In Parts I and II of this three-part historical series, the Dutch East India Company ship Amstelveen wrecked off Ras Madrakah in August 1763, leaving thirty barefoot castaways to march north across Bar Al Hikman. Kept alive by Omani fishermen who shared stone-well water, dates, fried fish, and coastal guides, twenty-two survivors walked into the harbor town of Sur after five grueling weeks.
detail.article_html:
Sur in September 1763 was a thriving maritime port known across the western Indian Ocean for its wooden dhow yards and seasoned deep-sea navigators. When the twenty-two sunburned, ragged Dutchmen limped into town along the shore road, local merchants and Sur's governor took them under protection at once. The castaways were given shaded quarters, steady meals, and clean cotton tunics to replace the salt-rotted rags they had worn since Ras Madrakah.

A Coastal Dhow Past the Cliffs of Qalhat

In Sur, the five-hundred-kilometer ordeal on foot finally ended. Rather than sending the weakened sailors overland across the Eastern Hajar mountain passes, town authorities arranged passage for all twenty-two men aboard an Omani coastal dhow bound for the capital.

Under a triangular lateen sail, the wooden vessel glided northwest along the Sea of Oman, passing the pale limestone ramparts of Qalhat and the coastal plain of Qurayyat before slipping between the dark volcanic headlands that guard the natural amphitheater of Old Muscat.

Sanctuary in Imam Ahmed bin Said's Muscat

The port the castaways entered in the autumn of 1763 reflected nineteen years of hard-won stability under Imam Ahmed bin Said Al Busaidi, who had unified Oman from Rustaq in November 1744 after expelling occupying Persian forces. Under his administration, Muscat functioned as an orderly international entrepôt where customs rules were enforced, sea lanes were policed, and merchant vessels called regularly from western India, the Gulf, East Africa, and Europe.

Brought before Muscat's authorities, third mate Cornelis Eyks and his twenty-one surviving crewmates were received with quiet dignity. Omani officials arranged safe lodging inside the port, medical care for their ulcerated feet and sun-ravaged skin, and daily rations while awaiting onward shipping. As regional trading vessels cleared harbor that season, the survivors were granted passage back toward Dutch East India Company stations in the Gulf and onward to Batavia and the Netherlands.

Two Centuries in a Quiet Bookshop

Throughout the wreck at Ras Madrakah, the burials along Bar Al Hikman, and the weeks among Omani fishing villages, Cornelis Eyks had protected his handwritten notes. Three years after reaching home, he published his eyewitness narrative in Amsterdam in 1766 under the title Noodlottige Gevallen van het Volk van 't Schip Amstelveen (The Fatal Misfortunes of the People of the Ship Amstelveen). Alongside the terror of the monsoon surf, Eyks set down in plain detail how unnamed Omani herders, fishermen, elders, and governors had saved twenty-two foreign strangers with well water, dates, cloth, and safe passage.

For more than two hundred and thirty years, that slim eighteenth-century Dutch pamphlet faded into obscurity until a surviving original copy turned up by chance in an antiquarian bookshop in southern France during the late 1990s. The find drew the attention of Dutch scholar Professor Dr. Klaas Doornbos, who spent years matching Eyks's daily entries against Dutch East India Company ship ledgers and walking the Omani coastline from Ras Madrakah to Sur.

Published in 2012 as Shipwreck and Survival in Oman, 1763 and translated into Arabic by Fatima Salim Al Ajmi in collaboration with Oman's Ministry of Heritage and Culture, the rediscovered logbook prompted joint maritime archaeology surveys off Ras Madrakah. More than two and a half centuries after the Amstelveen broke apart in the August fog, Eyks's pages remain the oldest known European eyewitness record of Oman's southern coast—preserved because coastal families chose to meet shipwrecked strangers with water and dates.

Sources

  • Cornelis Eyks, Noodlottige Gevallen van het Volk van 't Schip Amstelveen (1766)
  • Klaas Doornbos, Shipwreck and Survival in Oman, 1763 (translated into Arabic by Fatima Salim Al Ajmi in collaboration with the Ministry of Heritage and Culture)
detail.instagram_caption:
After five weeks of walking barefoot from the shipwreck reefs of Ras Madrakah across Bar Al Hikman, twenty-two surviving sailors from the Dutch East India Company ship Amstelveen limped into the maritime town of Sur in September 1763.

In Part III, the concluding chapter of our historical series, merchants and Sur's governor clothe and shelter the exhausted strangers before arranging their passage aboard an Omani coastal dhow past the limestone cliffs of Qalhat into the fortified bay of Old Muscat. Nineteen years after Imam Ahmed bin Said Al Busaidi unified the country at Rustaq, Muscat stood as an orderly Indian Ocean trade port where Omani authorities gave the castaways medical care, rations, and safe onward passage home.

Third mate Cornelis Eyks published his handwritten survival journal in Amsterdam in 1766, recording the Omani fishermen, villagers, and governors who kept twenty-two strangers alive. Forgotten for more than two centuries until a copy surfaced in a French bookshop in the late 1990s and was reconstructed by Professor Dr. Klaas Doornbos, the journal stands today as the oldest known European eyewitness record of southern Oman's coast.

Read the concluding chapter of the Amstelveen 1763 survival story at omanspire.om (link in bio).
